feed.title: Production journal — Moss Garden
feed.subtitle: One short story a day about how Moss Garden is made.

entry.title: Logging the guests who visit the garden in the codex
entry.summary: A look at the small visitors who pass through the garden, the codex that records them, and the rare ones you can collect.
entry.content:
Moss Garden, an idle game for iOS, has small guests who visit the garden, and the codex has a guests chip next to the plants where we write down who has stopped by. Now and then a special guest arrives with a golden or white tint, and as guests add up, decorations that dress the garden unlock. All of this only touches how the garden looks: dew, settlement and production don't change.

Guests stay in the codex

Guests visit even while the garden is empty. When you open the garden again, a single line in the welcome-back window shows who stopped by. On the guests chip in the codex, each guest card shows how many times they have visited and a dot if you have met a rare one. A short notice appears when a new or rare guest arrives.

Now and then a rare guest shows up

Very rarely, a guest arrives with a golden or white tint. The weather has nothing to do with it. We don't draw new art for these; we only change the guest's color, so even the same guest can look different the moment you meet them.

Collect enough and the garden gets a little brighter

When enough guests have visited, decorations such as halos of light, jars of fireflies and moonstones unlock, and unlocked decorations appear in the garden by themselves. They are cosmetic, and they don't earn you extra dew. So collecting at a relaxed pace costs you nothing.

FAQ

Do guests earn me more dew?

No. Guests and decorations only change how the garden looks; dew, settlement and production stay the same.

Do guests visit while the app is closed?

Yes. The guests who stopped by while the garden was empty show up as one line in the welcome-back window when you open it again.

entry.title: When the season changes, the plants in the garden change too
entry.summary: A cherry tree standing in a summer garden looks wrong, so we made each season fill the garden with its own plants.
entry.content:
In Moss Garden, an idle game for iOS, the plants you can grow change along with the season. The garden still has eight plant slots: four stay the same all year round, and the other four are filled by plants that bloom in the current season. Each slot keeps the same price and production per second, so the balance of the game doesn't change.

A cherry tree in summer looks wrong

The plant list used to stay the same no matter the season. That meant a summer garden could hold both a cherry tree, which blooms in spring, and a ginkgo, which turns gold in autumn. For a game built around seasons, a garden that looked out of season bothered us.

The slots stay, the plants in them change

We kept the order, the price and the production of the eight slots exactly as they were, and only changed which plant sits in a slot to match the season. Moss, fern, mushroom and bamboo are the base of Moss Garden, so they stay the same in every season. The other four slots (wildflowers, waterside plants, flowering trees and big trees) hold that season's plants in spring, summer, autumn and winter.

Plants from the last season move to the matching slot

If you still have a plant that is out of season, it is replanted as the in-season plant of the same slot, with the same number of plants. The slot's price and production are the same, so your income per second doesn't drop and the price of the next plant stays put. Losing nothing was the condition for doing it this way.

You can browse the codex by season

At the top of the codex there are spring, summer, autumn and winter chips, so you can look at the plants of each season. A plant that only blooms in another season is shown faded, with a note that you can plant it when that season comes. Plants that stand all year round carry an all-seasons mark. The season tab also tells you, before you change the season, that new plants will bloom in the next one.

FAQ

Do plants disappear when the season changes?

No. A plant that is out of season is replanted as the in-season plant of the same slot, with the same number of plants, so your income per second stays the same.

Does the price of plants change with the season?

No. The price and production of each slot stay the same whatever the season.

entry.title: The garden keeps growing when the app is closed
entry.summary: Moss Garden keeps collecting dew while the app is closed, and shows you what it earned when you return.
entry.content:
Moss Garden is a garden you look in on a few times a day. So it keeps growing even while the app is closed. When you come back, the welcome-back window shows the dew gathered in the meantime.

Time away is garden time too

A garden that only grows when you tap to water it wears you out, because you have to keep coming back. In Moss Garden, plants keep making dew while you are away.

The welcome-back window when you return

When you open the app again, a welcome-back window shows the dew gathered while you were away. Settlement has a cap, so even a long absence doesn't pile up without limit.

Turning the clock back doesn't settle

We also stopped the trick of turning the device clock back to collect rewards. When a clock rollback is detected, that stretch is not settled.

FAQ

If I leave the app closed for days, does the dew pile up forever?

No. Settlement has a cap, so even after a long time away, dew only builds up to that limit.

What kind of game is Moss Garden?

Moss Garden is an idle game for iOS. You plant and grow plants to gather dew.

entry.title: Why we keep two copies of the save
entry.summary: Losing a garden you've grown is the worst, so saves are split into a main file and a backup.
entry.content:
Moss Garden, an idle game for iOS, protects your garden with two safeguards: a checksum that detects a damaged save and a separate backup it restores from, with a notice. Turning the device clock back to collect rewards is also caught, and that stretch is not settled.

Two safeguards for the save

In an idle game, the most upsetting thing is losing the garden you've been growing. So saving has two safeguards.

The first is a checksum: a check value is written with the save, and if it doesn't match on load, the file is treated as damaged. The second is a backup: the main file and the backup are kept separately, so if the main file breaks we restore from the backup and tell you so. We were careful about the order, too, so a broken main file never overwrites a healthy backup.

Clock rollbacks

We also had to stop the trick of turning the device clock back to collect rewards. When a clock rollback is detected, that stretch is not settled, and the app tells you about it.

Keeping old saves working

When we add features, we keep the save format and only add new fields, so older saves still open in newer versions.

FAQ

What happens if the Moss Garden save file breaks?

The checksum notices the mismatch, the game restores from the separate backup and tells you it did.

Can I get rewards by changing the device clock?

No. When a clock rollback is detected, that stretch is not settled, and the app tells you about it.

entry.title: How the first TestFlight build went up
entry.summary: After finishing the MVP, the first internal build went up, but the deploy script stopped us once along the way.
entry.content:
The first MVP of Moss Garden, an idle game for iOS, went up to TestFlight as 1.0.0 (1) for internal testing after a deploy script stopped the first attempt. Processing took about three minutes, and the build was not submitted for review or opened to external testers.

What was in the MVP

The first MVP came together with eight plants, offline settlement, seasons, a collection book, saving and settings. We then uploaded it to TestFlight as 1.0.0 (1) for internal testing. Processing took about three minutes, and we did not submit it for review or open it to external testers.

The first attempt failed

When the deploy script ran the green gate, an environment variable meaning "don't bump the build number" leaked into the tests and broke them, and the script stopped right there. Thanks to that stop, no bad build was uploaded. We fixed it so child processes no longer inherit the outer environment, then uploaded again.

Deploys can be a hassle, but we keep the rule: if the tests aren't green, nothing ships.

FAQ

What was in the first Moss Garden TestFlight build?

Eight plants, offline settlement, seasons, a collection book, saving and settings, uploaded as 1.0.0 (1) for internal testing.

Has Moss Garden been submitted for App Store review?

No. This build was only uploaded for internal testing, and we did not submit it for review.

entry.title: The day we redrew the garden
entry.summary: After hearing the app looked rather dull overall, we reworked the garden screen from scratch.
entry.content:
We redrew the garden screen of Moss Garden, an idle game for iOS, after hearing that the design felt dull. It now has a deeper forest palette, a large garden scene with hills, a lotus pond and fireflies, and view-only decorations that never change the pace of the game.

Starting with color

The most honest feedback on the garden screen was that the design felt dull overall. So we started with color: a deeper forest background, with the moss and dew greens toned down so the screen stays easy on the eyes.

The garden scene

The top half of the screen is now a large garden scene: two layers of hills, a lotus pond, stars and a moon at night, fireflies at dusk, and a soft ripple when you water. A rounded panel below switches between plants and decorations.

Decorations

Decorations began with stepping stones, a fence, a bench and a stone lantern. They are for looking at only, so they have no effect on the pace of the game. Buying one places it in its spot right away, and moving it back and forth costs nothing.

Making things pretty never ends, so we stopped at one question: is this a screen you'd want to open every day?

FAQ

What changed on the Moss Garden garden screen?

The color palette, a large garden scene with hills, a lotus pond, stars, a moon and fireflies, and a panel that switches between plants and decorations.

Do decorations affect how the game plays?

No. Decorations are for looking at only, so they never change the pace of the idle game.

entry.title: Why show dew with decimals
entry.summary: The moss grows 0.1 per second, yet the dew counter looked frozen. This is how we fixed the number format.
entry.content:
Moss Garden is an idle (incremental) game for iOS, and its dew counter used to look frozen because it showed only whole numbers from ten upward. We now show two decimals below 1 and one decimal below 1,000, and we round down so the number never promises more than you have.

Why the number looked frozen

Moss was piling up at 0.1 per second, but the dew number at the top of the screen stayed the same for a long time. A tester told us they couldn't tell whether it was counting at all. The cause was simple: from ten upward we only showed whole numbers.

What we changed

Values below 1 now show two decimals, and values below 1,000 show one. Trailing zeros are dropped, so you read 289 instead of 289.0.

The one real decision was rounding. Showing 185.56 as 185.6 would make something you can't buy yet look affordable. So we round down instead: the number on screen is always at most what you actually have.

It is a tiny change, but in a game about waiting, watching the number move is part of the reward.

FAQ

Why does Moss Garden show dew with decimals?

Because the moss grows 0.1 per second, and whole numbers made the counter look frozen. Decimals let you see that it is counting.

Does the dew number round up or down?

Down. The number on screen is always at most the amount you actually have, so nothing looks affordable before it is.
